title: Smith v. Commissioner
subject: Funded Research Exclusion
summary: Smith v. Commissioner is a U.S. Tax Court ruling for architecture and engineering partnerships claiming the R&D tax credit under I.R.C. § 41. The court upheld the funded research regulation, found no contract made payment contingent on research success, allowed partial credits only where the firm retained substantial rights, and held partner compensation reasonable under § 174(e).

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background

The litigation in Adrian D. Smith & Nancy W. Smith, et al. v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue, Docket Nos. 13382-17, 13385-17, and 13387-17—encompassing both the United States Tax Court's pivotal Order denying the Commissioner's motion for summary judgment on December 18, 2024 (2024 U.S. Tax Ct. LEXIS 3136) and its subsequent post-trial Memorandum Opinion on June 16, 2026 (T.C. Memo. 2026-50)—represents a defining adjudication for architecture, engineering, and professional services firms claiming the federal research and development (R&D) tax credit under Internal Revenue Code (I.R.C.) § 41. Presided over by Judge Christian N. Weiler, these consolidated proceedings examine the intersection of international commercial design contracts, intellectual property vesting, choice-of-law mechanics under Tax Court Rule 146, administrative law deference following the Supreme Court's landmark ruling in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, and the reasonableness of pass-through partner compensation under I.R.C. § 174(e).
The Taxpayer's Claim and Factual Context

During the 2008, 2009, and 2010 taxable years, petitioners Adrian D. Smith, Carlisle G. Gill, and Robert J. Forest were the sole equity partners of Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture, LLP (AS+GG), an Illinois limited liability partnership headquartered in Chicago. AS+GG operates an internationally recognized architectural practice specializing in the design of high-performance, energy-efficient supertall buildings and urban masterplans, including designs intended to be among the world's tallest towers (such as the Atrium City Tower and the Kingdom Tower, the latter designed to exceed 1,001 meters and still under construction), while its founding partners had previously worked at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill on the Burj Khalifa, currently the world's tallest structure. Unlike a traditional linear design approach, AS+GG's operational methodology followed a holistic approach that engaged all elements of the project from the very beginning, with the firm working across all aspects of the building rather than delegating its work to engineers or other mechanics. To design these structures, the partnership performed research studies that, according to the Court's findings, included thermodynamics, geotechnics, fluid dynamics, microclimates, and plant acclimation (Masdar HQ), wind tunnel testing and load-carrying-capacity research for a tower built on sand (Kingdom Tower), solar orientation and wind movement analysis (Atrium City Tower), solar diagrams for sunshade and facade optimization (Plot 14), and the integration of wind turbines (Plot R2).

For the 2008, 2009, and 2010 tax years, AS+GG calculated and claimed federal research credits under I.R.C. § 41 in the amounts of $3,134,318, $557,455, and $515,463, respectively. Because AS+GG was structured as a flow-through partnership for federal income tax purposes, the research tax credits passed through to the individual partners' joint federal income tax returns and were carried forward and subsequently carried back through amendments to their original joint returns. A primary component of the claimed Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) for the 2008 taxable year consisted of partner wage QREs—originally claimed at $16,231,850, $5,883,329, and $2,574,321 for Messrs. Smith, Gill, and Forest, respectively—derived from the partners' 2008 compensation (AS+GG deducted guaranteed payments of $970,126, $855,994, and $788,621 and reported gross salaries of $30,249,440, $11,799,698, and $9,286,873), with the parties stipulating before trial that the partners devoted 53.66%, 45%, and 27.72% of their time, respectively, to qualified services.
The Tax Authority's Challenge and Procedural Evolution

Following an examination of the partnership and partner returns, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) disallowed the claimed I.R.C. § 41 research credits and, on April 7, 2017, issued Statutory Notices of Deficiency to the partners and their spouses, who timely filed petitions with the United States Tax Court that were consolidated for all purposes on February 28, 2018 (an undisputed change in accounting method made during the examination explains differences between the returns and the notices). To manage the complexity of AS+GG's project portfolio—credits attributable to 48 projects in total—the parties stipulated prior to trial to limit the trial to a sample of six major international design projects, with the findings to be projected on a pro rata basis to the remaining projects: Atrium City Tower (Project No. 208021, located in Dubai, United Arab Emirates), Kingdom Tower (Project No. 210005, located in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia), Masdar HQ (Project No. 208004, located in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates), Atrium City Masterplan (Project No. 207014, Dubai), Plot 14 (Project No. 206003, Dubai), and Plot R2 (Project No. 207016, Dubai).

Before trial, the parties entered into a Stipulation of Settled Issues (filed August 2, 2019) and a Supplemental Stipulation of Settled Issues containing several major concessions that significantly narrowed the issues before the Court. Most notably, the parties agreed that AS+GG's claimed business components satisfied the substantive four-part test for qualified research under I.R.C. § 41(d) and that the exclusions under § 41(d)(4)(A)–(G) were inapplicable, the IRS conceded accuracy-related penalties under § 6662(a), and the parties stipulated to the exact percentages of time each partner devoted to performing qualified research activities during 2008, and respondent separately stipulated total reasonable compensation for 2008 of $2.32 million, $1.807 million, and $1.474 million for Messrs. Smith, Gill, and Forest. In short, the IRS did not contest that AS+GG's research on the six sample projects satisfied the substantive four-part test for qualified research under I.R.C. § 41(d). Consequently, the Commissioner's challenge focused on two primary statutory exclusions and limitations: first, that all research performed by AS+GG pursuant to the six sample client contracts was disqualified as "funded research" within the meaning of I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d); and second, that the 2008 compensation allocated to the partners as QRE wages exceeded the amount that was "reasonable under the circumstances" under I.R.C. § 174(e).
Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

The legal controversy in Smith is governed by the interconnected provisions of I.R.C. §§ 41 and 174—the research credit having originated in the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 and been revised by the Tax Reform Act of 1986, and the § 174(e) reasonableness requirement having been added by the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1989—alongside longstanding Treasury Regulations (first proposed in 1983 and finalized in 1989) and federal appellate precedent. Section 41(a) and (b) allow taxpayers to claim a nonrefundable tax credit equal to 20 percent of the excess of current-year QREs over a statutory base amount, where QREs comprise in-house research expenses (wages and supplies) and 65 percent of eligible contract research expenses. Because partners in a service partnership do not employ themselves and do not receive traditional W-2 employee wages, I.R.C. § 41(b)(2)(D) cross-references I.R.C. § 401(c)(2) to define "wages" for self-employed individuals and partners as the partner's "earned income"—specifically, net earnings from self-employment derived from the trade or business in which the research is performed.

To qualify for the credit under I.R.C. § 41(d)(1), research activities must satisfy a cumulative four-part test. First, under the Section 174 test, expenditures must qualify as research or experimental expenditures under I.R.C. § 174, meaning costs incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business that represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product or process. (While the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 later required capitalization and five-year domestic or fifteen-year foreign amortization for Specified Research or Experimental expenditures beginning in 2022—a mandate subsequently reversed for domestic expenditures incurred after December 31, 2024, by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act [OBBBA], P.L. 119-21—the substantive eligibility criteria of § 174 and the reasonable compensation limitation of § 174(e) continuously govern § 41 credit claims). Second, under the technological-in-nature test, the research must fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Third, under the business component test, the discovered information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component (any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention held for sale, lease, or license, or used in the taxpayer's trade or business). Fourth, under the process-of-experimentation test, substantially all of the activities must constitute elements of a structured process of experimentation that evaluates one or more alternatives through modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error to resolve technical uncertainty.

Even where all four substantive tests of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1) are met, I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) expressly excludes from qualified research any research "to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person (or governmental entity)". Because the statute does not define the term "funded," Treasury promulgated Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) (applicable via cross-reference in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(9)), which directs courts to examine all agreements between the researcher and its client. Under this regulatory framework, research performed under a customer contract is treated as non-funded—and therefore fully eligible for the credit—only if two conjunctive criteria are satisfied: under Prong 1, payment to the researcher must be contingent on the success of the research, meaning the researcher bears the financial risk of technical failure; and under Prong 2, the researcher must retain substantial rights in the research results. Crucially, under the partial funding rules of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3) and (d)(2), if a taxpayer fails Prong 1 because contract payments are guaranteed or not contingent on technical success, but succeeds on Prong 2 because it retains substantial rights in the research results, the research is treated as funded only to the extent of the payments received from the client. In that scenario, the taxpayer remains legally entitled to claim a partial research credit to the extent its actual QREs incurred on the project exceed the payments received from the client. Conversely, if the taxpayer fails to retain substantial rights under Prong 2, the research is 100 percent disqualified regardless of whether the contractor suffered financial losses or cost overruns. Finally, I.R.C. § 174(e) restricts deductible and credit-eligible research expenditures to amounts that are "reasonable under the circumstances".
The Court's Two-Stage Holding

The Tax Court resolved the Smith litigation across two distinct procedural stages, demonstrating the sharp legal distinction between surviving a pretrial summary judgment motion and satisfying the affirmative burden of proof at trial.

In the first phase, the Commissioner filed a motion for summary judgment on October 1, 2024, asserting that under Tax Court Rule 121(a)(2) there were no genuine disputes of material fact and that all six sample projects constituted funded research as a matter of law. On December 18, 2024, Judge Weiler issued an Order denying the Commissioner's motion for summary judgment in its entirety. Drawing all factual inferences in the light most favorable to the non-moving taxpayers, the Court determined that summary adjudication was inappropriate because genuine issues of material fact and unsettled questions of foreign law remained across the sample contracts. Specifically, the Court noted that the contracts for Atrium City Tower, Plot 14, and Plot R2 implicated the laws of the United Arab Emirates under Tax Court Rule 146 regarding how intellectual property rights vested upon early termination. For Kingdom Tower, the Court observed that transferring ownership of specific deliverable drawings and copyrights did not automatically establish as a matter of law that AS+GG was divested of all substantial rights in its underlying technical know-how under Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000), nor had the Commissioner adequately briefed the interplay of payment contingencies. For Masdar HQ, competing contractual provisions granting AS+GG ownership of underlying intellectual property while restricting replication required evidentiary clarification at trial.

In the second phase, following the March 2025 trial in Chicago, Judge Weiler handed down the final Memorandum Opinion on June 16, 2026 (T.C. Memo. 2026-50), delivering a detailed split holding on the merits. First, the Court upheld the validity of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) in the wake of Loper Bright, ruling that statutory stare decisis and Skidmore persuasiveness foreclosed the petitioners' attempt to invalidate the two-pronged funded research regulation. Second, evaluating Prong 1 (financial risk / payment contingency), the Court ruled in favor of the Commissioner across all six sample projects, holding that none of AS+GG's contracts conditioned payment on the technical success of the research. Third, evaluating Prong 2 (retention of substantial rights), the Court divided the six projects based on their exact contractual IP provisions: for Kingdom Tower and Plot 14, the Court held that the contracts vested absolute ownership and copyright in the clients and required unrestricted client consent for reuse, completely disqualifying both projects from any § 41 credit. However, for the remaining four projects—Atrium City Tower, Masdar HQ, Atrium City Masterplan, and Plot R2—the Court held that AS+GG retained substantial rights to reuse the underlying research results. Consequently, under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3), the petitioners were held eligible for partial research credits on those four projects to the extent AS+GG's QREs exceeded the client payments received, although the Court stated it was unable to determine the precise amounts of these partial credits (if any) because there was insufficient evidence before it, and left the pro rata projection to AS+GG's remaining 42 projects to the parties, with additional briefing or further trial proceedings available if they cannot agree. Fourth, on the issue of 2008 partner compensation under I.R.C. § 174(e), the Court ruled in favor of the petitioners, applying the Seventh Circuit's independent investor test under Golsen to hold that the Partners' compensation claimed for 2008, in total, was reasonable.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

Although the IRS's pretrial concession removed the substantive four-part test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1) from dispute, the petitioners' inability to secure full research credits across their project portfolio resulted from six specific legal, contractual, and evidentiary failures under the funded research exclusion of I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d). Examining the progression from the December 2024 Summary Judgment Order to the June 2026 Memorandum Opinion exposes the exact structural vulnerabilities that ensnare architecture, engineering, and custom contracting firms during Tax Court litigation.
Failure 1: Misplaced Reliance on Administrative Law Invalidation Post-Loper Bright

Confronted with traditional architectural fee schedules that lacked explicit technical risk-shifting clauses, the petitioners attempted to bypass Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) altogether by challenging its validity under the Supreme Court's decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 144 S. Ct. 2244 (2024). Because Loper Bright overruled the Chevron doctrine and instructed federal courts to independently determine the single best meaning of statutory text, the petitioners argued that Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) is no longer the single best reading of I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H), that its two-element requirements of "contingent on success" and "substantial rights" are superfluous and not found in the Code, and that the Court should not defer to prior cases relying on the regulation because none performed the statutory-text analysis now required. Petitioners urged the Tax Court to discard Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) and interpret the statutory word "funded" according to its narrow dictionary definition as "a sum of money set apart for a specific objective," which would only exclude direct research grants or dedicated R&D subsidies rather than commercial fee-for-service design contracts.

Judge Weiler rejected this administrative law challenge on two decisive legal grounds. First, the Court applied the doctrine of statutory stare decisis, emphasizing the Supreme Court's explicit limiting language in Loper Bright that prior judicial holdings validating specific agency actions remain binding precedent notwithstanding the change in interpretive methodology. Because numerous federal decisions—including Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995), Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 42 Fed. Cl. 485 (1998) (which upheld the "substantial rights" element under Chevron), rev'd, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000), Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015), Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024), United States v. Grigsby, 86 F.4th 602 (5th Cir. 2023), and Dynetics, Inc. & Subs. v. United States, 121 Fed. Cl. 492 (2015)—as well as prior Tax Court precedent (Tangel v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-1; Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84; Union Carbide Corp. & Subs. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50; General Dynamics Corp. & Subs. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 1996-153) had relied on and applied Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), the Court held that those holdings remain in effect. Second, evaluating the regulation under Skidmore v. Swift & Co., 323 U.S. 134 (1944), the Tax Court found respondent's "power to persuade" argument compelling, noting that Treasury first proposed the regulations in 1983 in response to congressional concerns, finalized them in 1989, and has provided consistent guidance for some 35 years, that Congress delegated authority under § 7805(a), and that the guidance offers both clarity and certainty; it concluded the regulatory requirements are reasonably related to and consistent with the intent of § 41(d)(4)(H), which—as Fairchild explained—allocates the credit to the person bearing the financial risk of failure of the research. The Court further rejected petitioners' narrow reading of "funded," observing that the term can equally mean any research provided with financial resources or monetary support, and that petitioners' reading would in any event not be more beneficial to them than the regulation. Attempting to litigate around unfavorable contract terms by attacking the underlying Treasury Regulation proved wholly ineffective.
Failure 2: Conflating Professional "Proper Performance" with Technical "Successful Performance" (Prong 1 Failure Across All Six Projects)

To satisfy Prong 1 of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1) and establish that research is not funded, a taxpayer must prove that its contractual right to receive and retain payment is contingent upon the successful development of the uncertain technical result. While Judge Weiler gave the petitioners the benefit of the doubt at the summary judgment stage in December 2024 due to unresolved factual questions surrounding how contract milestone payments operated in practice, the petitioners failed at trial to carry their burden of proof on all six sample projects. The root cause of this failure was that AS+GG's contracts—each a fixed-price lump-sum engagement (approximately $298 million for Atrium City Tower, $29 million for Kingdom Tower, $18.7 million for Masdar HQ, $750,000 for Atrium City Masterplan, $10.23 million for Plot 14, and $7.5 million for Plot R2)—utilized standard professional service billing mechanics: invoice-based monthly or phase payments tied to percentage of completion, clauses barring clients from delaying payment of undisputed invoice items, hourly or lump-sum fees for additional services, and reimbursable expense provisions, without conditioning payment on achieving uncertain engineering metrics.

At trial, the petitioners sought to analogize their contracts to Fairchild Industries, arguing that client approval gates at the conclusion of sequential design phases made payment contingent on research success. Specifically, in the Atrium City Tower contract (which required designing three of the world's tallest, highly energy-efficient towers in Dubai for client Meraas), petitioners relied on Schedule 2, Appendix B, which required AS+GG to "[d]evelop the concept design schemes culminating in a concept design approved by [Meraas]," "obtain agreement of the design program[] with [Meraas]," and "incorporate as applicable the requirements of [Meraas] and submit to the [Meraas] for approval purposes the final version of the Detailed Design Phase documentation". Similarly, in the Masdar HQ contract, petitioners pointed to the requirement of a "complete performance evaluation of the systems to review if Project goals are being met" at the end of Phase 1, Masdar's right not to proceed with AS+GG for Phase 2, and the contract's "zero carbon emissions" and "minimal energy usage" requirements as the standard of success.

The Tax Court identified a fatal analytical flaw in the petitioners' argument: relying on Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024), and Geosyntec, it distinguished proper performance under a general professional standard of care from successful performance—meeting detailed barometers of success. In Fairchild Industries, the contract contained over 1,000 pages of technical specifications requiring the taxpayer to meet specific design, construction, quality, and performance standards, a clause by which the taxpayer accepted total responsibility for the research, and inspection terms allowing the work to be rejected, so that the taxpayer had no right to payment until it fully succeeded in each phase. Conversely, AS+GG's contracts merely obligated the firm to deliver designs following a general schedule of project details (with even the eight-page Kingdom Tower specification framed largely as flexible "recommendations") and conforming to general standards such as "sound internationally recognized professional standards" with reasonable "skill, care and diligence" or "Good Industry Practice," and contained neither a rejection clause based on failure to deliver a "successful" design nor any express acceptance of responsibility for producing the product.

Furthermore, the payment and termination clauses in AS+GG's contracts did not establish financial risk. In Masdar HQ, Section 12.3 explicitly stated that upon termination, "Masdar shall pay [AS+GG] the proportion of the price payable for the Services as relates to the work properly and satisfactorily carried out or where the Services are charged on a time basis, for the time properly and necessarily spent on the Services prior to the termination". Citing Geosyntec Consultants, Judge Weiler held that payment schedules tied to the percentage of services performed and payable on invoice, without prior review and approval of the work product, indicate funded research; citing Dynetics, Inc. & Subsidiaries v. United States, 121 Fed. Cl. 492 (2015), the Court held that reimbursable expenses and additional-service fees likewise do not show that financial risk was contingent on research success, and that the general risk of costs exceeding a lump-sum fee is a risk of doing business rather than of research failure. Applying Dynetics to the termination clauses (including Masdar's Section 12.3), the Court also clarified that the commercial risk of early project cancellation, or the "loss of profit opportunity" on unperformed future design phases, does not constitute the financial risk of research failure contemplated by Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1).
Failure 3: Ineffectiveness of Post-Hoc Settlement Agreements to Retroactively Shift Financial Risk

Because several of AS+GG's Middle Eastern projects were never completed, the firm executed settlement instruments with its clients, including a Deed of Settlement dated December 15, 2009, covering both Atrium City Tower and Atrium City Masterplan, a Settlement Agreement dated May 24, 2011, for Masdar HQ, and a final settlement documented in email correspondence and an October 10, 2010 acceptance letter for Plot 14 (no settlement was ever reached on Plot R2). Petitioners argued at trial that these settlement instruments modified the original design contracts and demonstrated that AS+GG had to accept compromised fee payouts, thereby proving that its compensation was contingent and financially at risk.

The Tax Court—which had stated in an Order served March 7, 2025, that settlement agreements modifying the original contract terms are not extrinsic evidence—rejected this theory by applying settled Seventh Circuit contract modification principles established in Large v. Mobile Tool International, Inc., 724 F.3d 766 (7th Cir. 2013), and Curia v. Nelson, 587 F.3d 824 (7th Cir. 2009). Under these authorities, an original contract remains in force only to the extent that it is not modified by the new agreement, so a settlement discharges original duties only insofar as they are inconsistent with it. Examining the text of the settlement documents, the Court observed that the Atrium City Tower Deed of Settlement did not discharge all original contractual terms, overriding only directly contradictory provisions. Even more decisively, the Masdar HQ Settlement Agreement contained an express preservation clause stating: "For the avoidance of doubt, the [original contract] remains in full force and effect subject to the terms of this Settlement Agreement and any amendments or variations to the [original contract]". Because these settlement instruments merely fixed a reasonable settlement payment for the portion of the work completed and terminated further obligations, while leaving the underlying non-contingent payment terms intact, they failed to convert funded service agreements into at-risk research contracts; AS+GG's inability to earn its full fee was merely a lost opportunity for profit under Dynetics. (The Atrium City Tower Deed of Settlement did, however, matter for Prong 2, as discussed under Failure 4.)
Failure 4: Unconditional Assignment of Intellectual Property and Unrestricted Client Consent Clauses (Prong 2 Failure on Kingdom Tower and Plot 14)

Under Prong 2 of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1) and (2), a researcher fails to retain "substantial rights" in its research if the contract confers upon the client the exclusive right to exploit the research results, or if the researcher must pay for the right to use the research results, and—under Tangel and Dynetics—a requirement to secure the client's permission to use the research, with no conditions limiting the client's ability to withhold consent, likewise defeats substantial rights. While AS+GG successfully retained substantial rights in four of its sample contracts (Atrium City Tower, Masdar HQ, Atrium City Masterplan, and Plot R2), it suffered complete disqualification on Kingdom Tower and Plot 14 due to uncompromising IP assignment and client-consent clauses.

In the December 18, 2024 Summary Judgment Order, Judge Weiler had declined to grant summary judgment on Kingdom Tower because the Commissioner had not adequately addressed whether transferring copyright in specific deliverable drawings under Section 6.1 divested AS+GG of all substantial rights in its underlying engineering know-how under Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d at 1374–75. However, once the full evidentiary record was examined at trial under the strict contract-terms standard of Tangel v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-1, Lockheed Martin, 210 F.3d at 1376, Dynetics, 121 Fed. Cl. at 521, and Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84, the Court found the Kingdom Tower and Plot 14 contracts unambiguous: under Sections 6.1(b) and (c), all information, data, drawings, and documents became the absolute property of the clients (for Kingdom Tower, provided the client fulfilled its remuneration obligations), and copyright in them vested in the clients, except for standard specifications, details, and designs previously used on other projects. Crucially, both contracts barred AS+GG from using the documents for any purpose other than performing the Services, and Section 6.2 required AS+GG to obtain the client's express prior written approval on each occasion to use the information for any other purpose, with no contractual condition limiting the client's ability to withhold that consent. The Tax Court held that requiring a researcher to obtain prior client permission to reuse research results—where the client possesses unfettered discretion to deny consent—precludes the retention of substantial rights and leaves the firm with mere incidental "institutional knowledge".

By contrast, in Atrium City Tower, the original contract standing alone would not have sufficed: the Court found Section 6.1 (termination-based IP vesting, the 25%-of-original-design-fee remuneration if Meraas replicated the project under 6.1(g), and the consent-based publication right under 6.1(h)) inapplicable on the facts, and Section 6.2(a) prohibited AS+GG from using project information for any other purpose without Meraas's express prior written approval on each occasion—a restriction that, under Dynetics and Tangel, would defeat substantial rights. However, Section 3.2(d)(ii) of the December 15, 2009 Deed of Settlement superseded Section 6.2(a), providing that AS+GG "retains the copyright in the Projects Documents" and grants Meraas only a license to market them with AS+GG credited; because that license did not restrict AS+GG's future use of its research, AS+GG retained substantial rights under the contract as amended. In Masdar HQ, Clause 10.1 provided that the Documents remained vested in AS+GG, Clause 10.2 granted Masdar a worldwide, irrevocable, royalty-free exclusive license to use the Documents for any purpose connected with the Project, and Clause 10.3 preserved AS+GG's right to publish articles; the Court held that Section 10.4—which barred AS+GG, absent Masdar's consent in its sole discretion, from using the Documents to design a structure similar in overall design and appearance to Masdar city or for other Masdar city purposes—did not prevent AS+GG from using functional technology developed through its research in a building of different overall design and appearance. For Atrium City Masterplan and Plot R2, the contracts provided that AS+GG retained the copyright in its work and granted the client only a license to reproduce it in connection with completing the project. Because "[t]he right to use the research results, even without the exclusive right, is a substantial right" under Lockheed Martin, AS+GG satisfied Prong 2 on Atrium City Tower, Masdar HQ, Atrium City Masterplan, and Plot R2.
Failure 5: Evidentiary Failure of Foreign Law Defenses Under Tax Court Rule 146

A major procedural battle in Smith revolved around the petitioners' attempt to invoke foreign law under the contracts' choice-of-law clauses—the laws of the Emirate of Dubai/U.A.E. (Atrium City Tower, Atrium City Masterplan, Plot 14, Plot R2), the laws of England, including the U.K. Sale of Goods Act 1979 (Masdar HQ), and the Copyright Laws of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (Kingdom Tower)—to establish both payment contingency and retained IP rights. Under Tax Court Rule 146, a litigant intending to raise an issue of foreign law must provide written notice, and the Court's determination of foreign law is treated as a ruling on a question of law supported by expert testimony, affidavits, and extracts of foreign legal authorities.

In the December 18, 2024 Summary Judgment Order, Judge Weiler rejected the Commissioner's procedural objection that petitioners had failed to give timely Rule 146 notice, observing that the IRS was long aware that the projects were located in the UAE and governed by UAE choice-of-law clauses, and therefore suffered no prejudice. Because determining how foreign law interacted with the contracts required evidentiary development, the Court denied summary judgment on Atrium City Tower, Plot 14, and Plot R2. By Order served March 7, 2025, the Court granted petitioners' request for judicial notice of the foreign law provisions and, in the Memorandum Opinion, declined respondent's renewed Rule 146 request to reconsider that Order as to the Atrium City Tower Contract. However, at trial, the petitioners' substantive reliance on foreign law failed completely, particularly on Kingdom Tower and Plot 14. On Prong 1, the Court distinguished System Technologies, Inc. v. Commissioner (where Indiana law supplied a refund remedy because the contract lacked an adequate remedy), holding that the Dubai contracts themselves provided adequate remedies, and found petitioners offered no explanation or expert testimony on how the U.K. sale-of-goods law—addressed to goods rather than services—would override the Masdar HQ terms. On Prong 2, petitioners contended that Saudi copyright moral rights (Kingdom Tower) and U.A.E. automatic author protections (Plot 14) overrode the contractual assignment of IP, but offered no caselaw or testimony explaining how. In the June 2026 Memorandum Opinion, Judge Weiler rejected this argument, holding under Lockheed Martin and Tangel that substantial-rights determinations must be made by reference to the research agreements between the parties, and adding that even if the U.A.E. law applied, its automatic protections would have been legally contracted away. Background provisions of foreign statutes not expressly incorporated into the agreement cannot be used to override unambiguous contract clauses that vest absolute ownership of the research in the client.
Failure 6: Computational and Cost-Accounting Deficiencies in Proving Excess QREs for Partial Credits

Because AS+GG failed Prong 1 (payment contingency) on all six projects but satisfied Prong 2 (substantial rights) on four projects (Atrium City Tower, Masdar HQ, Atrium City Masterplan, and Plot R2), the petitioners' sole pathway to recovery was the partial research credit provision of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3). Under this rule, when a taxpayer retains substantial rights under a non-contingent contract, the research is treated as funded only to the extent of client payments received, allowing the taxpayer to claim a research credit on the excess of its project QREs over client receipts.

At the conclusion of the trial, however, the petitioners faced an evidentiary roadblock: the Court stated that it was unable to determine the precise amounts of these partial credits (if any) because there was insufficient evidence before it to decide the issue. The opinion does not elaborate on which specific cost or billing records were missing; it simply makes clear that the excess of research expenses over payments received on the four qualifying projects was not established on the record. As a result, Judge Weiler did not compute the credit amounts in the June 2026 opinion; consistent with the parties' August 2, 2019 Stipulation of Settled Issues, the findings on the six sample projects are to be projected by the parties on a pro rata basis to AS+GG's remaining 42 projects, and the Court will entertain a request for additional briefing or further trial proceedings if the parties cannot agree.
Contrasting Evidentiary Triumph: Defeating the IRS's § 174(e) Reasonable Compensation Challenge

In stark contrast to their contractual deficiencies under the funded research exclusion, the petitioners achieved a complete victory on the reasonableness of their 2008 partner compensation under I.R.C. §§ 41(b)(2)(D) and 174(e). AS+GG's 2008 wage QREs for the partners were based on the partners' 2008 compensation (originally reported gross salaries of $30,249,440, $11,799,698, and $9,286,873 against total 2008 ordinary business income of $56,976,935) and the stipulated percentages of time spent on qualified services. The IRS challenged the resulting multi-million-dollar wage QREs under I.R.C. § 174(e), arguing that the independent investor test relates to § 162 rather than § 174 and that the Mayson Manufacturing multifactor test applied, under which its expert, Joseph J. Ruble, concluded reasonable compensation was approximately $2.3 million, $1.807 million, and $1.474 million (petitioners' expert, Brent M. Longnecker, concluded approximately $23.6–27.2 million, $11.7 million, and $9.5 million).

Because the parties stipulated that the cases are appealable to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit, the petitioners invoked the Golsen rule (Golsen v. Commissioner, 54 T.C. 742 (1970)) to bind the Tax Court to Seventh Circuit precedent in Exacto Spring Corp. v. Commissioner, 196 F.3d 833 (7th Cir. 1999). Under Exacto Spring, the Seventh Circuit applies the independent investor test, which creates a rebuttable presumption that an owner-employee's compensation is reasonable if investors obtain a far higher return than they had any reason to expect—a presumption rebutted if the return is attributable to an extraneous event rather than the manager's efforts; the Court noted that respondent's reliance on Suder ignored that the Mayson factors were applied there because that case was appealable to the Fifth Circuit. Although Mr. Ruble opined that the independent investor test should not apply under § 174(e), he nonetheless applied it in his own report—normalizing operating income, assuming hypothetical tax distributions at a 36.95% rate, and computing average equity of $545,000—and concluded that it yielded a 939 percent return on equity to the partners and that their total compensation was not unreasonable. Because the parties did not dispute that the mathematical results of the independent investor test support the compensation, Judge Weiler held that the Partners' compensation claimed for 2008, in total, is reasonable under I.R.C. § 174(e).
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following Markdown table maps each statutory, regulatory, and procedural requirement addressed in Smith v. Commissioner (covering both the December 18, 2024 Summary Judgment Order and the June 16, 2026 Post-Trial Memorandum Opinion) against the taxpayer's specific factual or legal deficiency, the Tax Court's governing standard of proof, and the final judicial disposition.

headers: Court's Standard of Proof & Analytical Framework
Final Judicial Holding (2024 Order vs. 2026 Opinion)

cells: 1. Validity of Funded Research Regulations
I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d); Loper Bright Enters. v. Raimondo, 144 S. Ct. 2244 (2024); Skidmore v. Swift & Co., 323 U.S. 134 (1944).

Petitioners argued post-Loper Bright that Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) is invalid because the two-prong test is not the "single best reading" of "funded," urging a narrow dictionary definition ("money set apart for a specific objective").

Statutory stare decisis preserves prior holdings relying on the regulation (Fairchild, Lockheed Martin, Geosyntec, Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Grigsby, Dynetics, Tangel, Betz). Under Skidmore, 35 years of consistent Treasury guidance carries strong persuasive weight.
Regulation Sustained in Full (2026 Opinion): The Tax Court rejected the Loper Bright challenge and upheld Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) as the controlling legal standard.
2. Financial Risk / Payment Contingency (Prong 1)

I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1); Fairchild Indus., Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995); Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015); Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Comm'r, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024); Dynetics, 121 Fed. Cl. 492 (2015).

Fixed-price lump-sum contracts used invoice-based percentage-of-completion payments, additional-service fees, and reimbursable expenses (e.g., Atrium City Tower Sched. 2 App. B; Masdar HQ Sec. 12.3 paying for "time properly and necessarily spent" prior to termination). Taxpayer conflated professional standard of care with technical risk.

2024 Order (Rule 121): Factual inferences drawn in favor of non-movant; ambiguity in payment terms barred summary judgment. 2026 Trial: Burden on taxpayer to prove by preponderance of evidence that payment depended on achieving uncertain technical specifications ("successful performance"), not mere professional care ("proper performance").
2024 Order: IRS Summary Judgment Denied. 2026 Opinion: Failed Across All 6 Projects. None of the contracts made payment contingent on research success; clients bore the financial risk of failure.
3. Contract Modification via Dispute Settlements
Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1); Large v. Mobile Tool Int'l, Inc., 724 F.3d 766 (7th Cir. 2013); Curia v. Nelson, 587 F.3d 824 (7th Cir. 2009).

Petitioners relied on the Atrium City Tower/Masterplan Deed of Settlement, the Masdar HQ Settlement Agreement, and the Plot 14 settlement emails to argue that partial fee payouts proved payments were contingent. However, the settlements only fixed payment for work completed and ended further obligations; the Masdar agreement expressly kept the original contract in full force.

Under Seventh Circuit contract law, a subsequent settlement agreement modifies an original contract only to the extent its terms are explicitly inconsistent with the original agreement. Loss of future profit opportunity is not research risk.

Rejected (2026 Opinion): Settlement deeds did not retroactively alter the original non-contingent fee structures or shift technical risk to AS+GG (though the Deed of Settlement's copyright clause did supersede Atrium City Tower Sec. 6.2(a) for Prong 2).
4. Retention of Substantial Rights (Prong 2)

Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1)–(2); Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000); Dynetics, 121 Fed. Cl. 492 (2015); Betz v. Comm'r, T.C. Memo. 2023-84; Tangel v. Comm'r, T.C. Memo. 2021-1.

Failure on 2 Projects: Kingdom Tower and Plot 14 (Secs. 6.1(b)–(c), 6.2) made all information, data, drawings, and documents the client's absolute property, vested copyright in the client, and required express prior written client approval on each occasion (without conditions on withholding consent) for AS+GG to use results. Success on 4 Projects: Atrium City Tower (Deed of Settlement § 3.2(d)(ii) superseding Sec. 6.2(a)), Masdar HQ (Cl. 10.1–10.3), Atrium City Masterplan, and Plot R2 (copyright retained by AS+GG) retained underlying IP and granted only project-specific licenses.

2024 Order: Citing Lockheed Martin, transferring specific drawing copyrights does not automatically divest all substantial rights as a matter of law. 2026 Trial: Express contract terms control (Tangel; Lockheed Martin). Taxpayer bears the burden and must retain at least a non-exclusive right to use research results without paying royalties or seeking unrestricted client consent.

2024 Order: IRS Summary Judgment Denied. 2026 Opinion: Split Holding. Disqualified on Kingdom Tower and Plot 14 (0% credit). Satisfied on Atrium City Tower, Masdar HQ, Atrium City Masterplan, and Plot R2.
5. Foreign Law Application to IP Rights
Tax Court Rule 146; Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d); Lockheed Martin, 210 F.3d at 1375–76; Dynetics, 121 Fed. Cl. at 514; Tangel v. Comm'r, T.C. Memo. 2021-1.

Petitioners invoked Dubai/U.A.E. law (Atrium City Tower, Masterplan, Plot 14, Plot R2), U.K. law including the Sale of Goods Act 1979 (Masdar HQ), and Saudi copyright moral rights (Kingdom Tower), arguing these established payment contingency and overrode contractual IP transfers to clients, without caselaw or expert testimony explaining how.

2024 Order: Under Rule 146, foreign law is a question of law requiring expert evidence; summary judgment premature. 2026 Trial: Judicial notice of foreign law granted (Order served Mar. 7, 2025); funded research inquiry looks strictly to the agreements between the parties; foreign statutes not expressly incorporated cannot override unambiguous contract terms that provide adequate remedies (distinguishing System Technologies).

2024 Order: Allowed foreign law issues to proceed to trial. 2026 Opinion: Rejected. Foreign law did not establish payment contingency on any project and cannot override express contractual divestment of IP in Plot 14 and Kingdom Tower; U.A.E. protections would in any event have been contracted away.
6. Partial Credit Computation (Excess QREs over Payments)
Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3) & (6) (ex. 1); Stipulation of Settled Issues (Aug. 2, 2019) pro rata projection.
The record contained insufficient evidence for the Court to determine the precise amounts of the partial credits (if any), i.e., the excess of research expenses over payments received.

When Prong 1 fails (non-contingent payment) but Prong 2 succeeds (substantial rights retained), taxpayer must substantiate that project-specific QREs exceeded total contract/settlement payments received from the client.

Partial Credit Allowed in Principle (2026 Opinion): Allowed for the 4 qualifying projects to the extent QREs exceeded payments; amounts not determined; pro rata projection to the remaining 42 projects left to the parties, with additional briefing or further trial available if they cannot agree.
7. Partner Wage QRE Reasonableness
I.R.C. §§ 41(b)(2)(D), 174(e), 401(c)(2); Golsen v. Comm'r, 54 T.C. 742 (1970); Exacto Spring Corp. v. Comm'r, 196 F.3d 833 (7th Cir. 1999).

No taxpayer failure. IRS challenged 2008 partner compensation underlying the wage QREs as excessive using the Mayson multifactor test. Respondent's own expert's independent investor calculation yielded a 939% return on equity, and the parties did not dispute those mathematical results.

Under the Golsen rule, Seventh Circuit's independent investor test (Exacto Spring) governs. A high rate of return to an inactive independent investor creates a strong rebuttable presumption that compensation is reasonable.
Taxpayer Victory (2026 Opinion): Respondent's expert computed a 939% return on equity; the Partners' 2008 compensation, in total, held reasonable under § 174(e).
8. Substantive Four-Part Test & Partner Time Allocation

No trial failure in Smith because the IRS stipulated to partner time percentages and conceded the § 41(d) four-part test pretrial (contrast with Phoenix Design Group, T.C. Memo. 2024-113, where vague time tracking and lack of technical uncertainty proved fatal).

Taxpayer must demonstrate technical uncertainty and a structured process of experimentation relying on hard sciences at the business component level, supported by nexus between wages and qualified activities.
Conceded by IRS Pretrial: Satisfied via pretrial stipulation on the 6 sample projects.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the Tax Court's rulings in Smith v. Commissioner into concrete legal, contractual, and engineering compliance protocols, the following two applied industry case studies examine realistic commercial projects confronting the exact legal traps exposed by Judge Weiler's December 2024 Order and June 2026 Memorandum Opinion. Each case study sets forth a step-by-step remedial restructuring across project governance, technical documentation, contract drafting, and financial experimentation tracking.
Case Study 1: Structural & Environmental Engineering LLP — Supertall Megastructure & Microclimate Wind-Vortex Mitigation Project
Baseline Project Scenario and Identified Smith Pitfalls

Vanguard Tall-Structure Engineering LLP ("Vanguard"), a Chicago-based limited liability partnership of structural and environmental engineers (whose tax disputes are appealable to the Seventh Circuit), is engaged by a Middle Eastern sovereign real estate developer ("Sovereign DevCo") to engineer a 950-meter mixed-use supertall tower in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, for a total contract price of $18 million. The tower's architectural geometry necessitates an unprecedented exterior diagrid structural exoskeleton and an active double-skin thermodynamic facade capable of mitigating severe desert wind-vortex shedding while reducing mechanical cooling loads by 40 percent.

Under Vanguard's initial draft agreement, modeled on standard international architectural and engineering service templates, the partnership faces three acute legal vulnerabilities identified in Smith. First, regarding Prong 1 (financial risk), Vanguard bills monthly on a percentage-of-completion basis across five design phases (Concept, Schematic, Detailed Design, Construction Documents, and Site Supervision), plus reimbursable wind-tunnel testing costs. Progression between phases requires Sovereign DevCo's written approval of phase deliverables, and Vanguard warrants that its engineering services will conform to "the prevailing standard of reasonable skill, care, and diligence practiced by international structural engineering firms." In the event of early contract termination, Sovereign DevCo is obligated to pay Vanguard for "all services properly performed and time necessarily expended prior to the termination date." Under the Tax Court's holdings on Atrium City Tower and Masdar HQ, this payment structure guarantees failure under Prong 1 of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1) because payment is tied to "proper performance" under a professional standard of care and time expended rather than the achievement of uncertain technical specifications.

Second, regarding Prong 2 (substantial rights), Article 8.1 of the draft contract states that "all drawings, BIM models, wind-tunnel datasets, structural calculations, and copyrights created hereunder shall vest absolutely in Sovereign DevCo upon payment of each monthly invoice, and Vanguard shall not utilize any project data or designs for any other client without Sovereign DevCo's prior written consent." Furthermore, the agreement contains a Saudi Arabian choice-of-law clause. Under the Tax Court's rulings on Kingdom Tower and Plot 14, Article 8.1 completely divests Vanguard of substantial rights because the client has unfettered discretion to withhold consent for reuse, and Vanguard cannot invoke foreign statutory copyright protections under Tax Court Rule 146 to override express contractual terms. Third, regarding QRE accounting, Vanguard's three equity partners receive $4.5 million each in guaranteed payments and self-employment distributive shares, but record their hours against a single macro project code ("Project 2026-Riyadh") without segregating qualified R&D cost overruns from routine CAD production expenses.
Step 1: Restructuring Contract Terms to Establish Financial Risk (Prong 1 Remediation)

To satisfy Prong 1 of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1) and align the engagement with Fairchild Industries rather than Geosyntec Consultants, Vanguard must eliminate time-basis billing and standard-of-care progress payments for the experimental engineering phases and replace them with objective Technical Performance Milestone Acceptance Criteria coupled with an unconditional fee-refund remedy. First, Vanguard's tax and legal counsel must sever the $18 million master agreement into two distinct contractual schedules: Schedule A (Experimental Engineering & Prototype Validation Phases — $11 million Fixed At-Risk Price), covering Concept, Schematic, and Detailed Engineering modeling, and Schedule B (Routine Construction Documentation & Site Administration — $7 million Time-and-Materials Price), isolating all credit-eligible research exclusively within Schedule A.

Second, Vanguard must attach a quantitative Technical Performance Specification Annex (Annex 1) to Schedule A that defines concrete, uncertain engineering benchmarks rather than aesthetic or code-compliance checklists (specifically requiring the structure to achieve a wind-induced peak lateral acceleration at the 900-meter occupied level of [image1] under a 50-year return period boundary-layer wind tunnel test while maintaining a structural steel tonnage ratio of [image2] and a facade solar heat gain coefficient of [image3]). Third, Vanguard must replace the standard phase-approval and termination-for-time-spent clauses in Schedule A with the following legally enforceable risk-allocation provision:

"Clause 4.2 (Contingent Technical Acceptance & Financial Risk Allocation): Notwithstanding any general professional standard of care, Contractor [Vanguard] acknowledges and agrees that its right to earn and retain Compensation under Schedule A is strictly contingent upon the technical success of the Engineering Research Deliverables in satisfying every quantitative performance metric set forth in Annex 1 (Technical Benchmarks). Any interim progress draws advanced prior to final Schedule A validation shall constitute refundable conditional advances. In the event any Schedule A Deliverable fails to achieve the Annex 1 Technical Benchmarks during independent wind-tunnel or thermodynamic validation, Client [Sovereign DevCo] shall have the absolute right to reject the Deliverable, withhold milestone payments, require Contractor to re-engineer and re-test the system solely at Contractor's uncompensated cost and expense, or terminate Schedule A for technical failure and demand a full refund of all conditional advances previously paid for the failed system. Upon any termination prior to technical validation of the Annex 1 Benchmarks, Contractor shall not be entitled to compensation for time spent, quantum meruit, reimbursable expenses, or work properly performed on unvalidated deliverables."
Step 2: Restructuring Intellectual Property and Governing Law Clauses (Prong 2 Remediation)

To avoid the fatal IP forfeiture suffered in Kingdom Tower and Plot 14 and replicate the successful IP retention posture of Atrium City Tower and Masdar HQ, Vanguard must explicitly separate ownership of the site-specific architectural rendering from the underlying engineering methodologies, computational scripts, and structural research results. Rather than relying on foreign copyright statutes under Tax Court Rule 146, Vanguard must embed the exact parameters of its retained rights directly within Article 8 of the executed contract so that the four corners of the agreement satisfy Lockheed Martin, Dynetics, and Tangel. Specifically, Vanguard must redraft Article 8.1 as follows:

"Clause 8.1 (Retention of Substantial Rights in Research Results): All Underlying Engineering Intellectual Property—including but not limited to structural diagrid optimization algorithms, computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulation scripts, wind-vortex damping geometries, thermodynamic facade cavity assemblies, structural node calculations, and engineering know-how developed, discovered, or refined by Contractor during the performance of the Services ('Research Results')—shall remain vested solely and exclusively in Contractor. Upon full payment of the Contract Price, Contractor grants Client a perpetual, royalty-free, irrevocable license to use the final deliverable construction drawings strictly for the physical construction, operation, and maintenance of the Project on the designated Riyadh Site. While Contractor covenants not to construct an identical visual exterior architectural replica of the building silhouette within a 100-kilometer radius of Riyadh, Contractor retains the absolute, non-exclusive, perpetual, and royalty-free right to use, adapt, publish, and commercially exploit all Research Results, structural systems, and engineering methodologies on any other project worldwide without requiring prior notice to, or consent from, Client, and without payment of any royalty or fee."
Step 3: Restructuring Project Governance and Technical Experimentation Documentation

Although the IRS conceded the substantive four-part test of I.R.C. § 41(d)(1) prior to trial in Smith, contemporary Tax Court decisions—most notably Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113—demonstrate that engineering firms face aggressive audit disallowances when they fail to substantiate technical uncertainty and a structured process of experimentation at the sub-component level, while Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024), on which the Smith Court relied for its Prong 1 analysis, shows that engineering design contracts lacking Fairchild-level specificity are treated as funded research. To insulate the Riyadh project against a substantive § 41(d) challenge, Vanguard's project governance committee must establish a formal Business Component Hierarchy under the shrinking-back rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) prior to commencing design work.

Rather than treating the entire 950-meter tower as a single monolithic business component, project leadership must partition Schedule A into discrete engineering sub-components: Sub-Component 2026-A (High-Altitude Diagrid Node Fatigue and Outrigger Damping Geometry), Sub-Component 2026-B (Pressurized Double-Skin Facade Thermodynamic Cavity), and Sub-Component 2026-C (Mat Foundation Karst-Limestone Load-Transfer Matrix). For each sub-component, the principal engineer must author a contemporaneous Technical Uncertainty Charter explaining why existing building codes (such as IBC and ASCE 7) and standard engineering formulas cannot achieve the Annex 1 benchmarks. Throughout the design phases, engineers must maintain chronological simulation logs documenting each hypothesis tested, the specific finite element analysis (FEA) and CFD modeling runs executed, the quantitative results of failed design iterations, and the final empirical wind-tunnel validation data.
Step 4: Experimentation Cost Accounting and Partner Compensation Substantiation

To protect the partnership under both the partial credit rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3) (as a secondary fallback defense) and the reasonable compensation mandate of I.R.C. § 174(e), Vanguard must overhaul its internal time and cost accounting. First, Vanguard must configure its job-cost accounting ledger to track all Schedule A qualified expenditures—comprising employee W-2 wages, partner earned income, wind-tunnel prototype supplies, and 65 percent of domestic sub-consultant testing fees—strictly by sub-component code against conditional milestone receipts. If Vanguard incurs $12.8 million in verified QREs on Schedule A while receiving $11.0 million in client payments, the segregated ledger provides immediate, audit-ready proof of $1.8 million in unfunded excess QREs under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3), avoiding the unresolved computation left in Smith, where the Court found insufficient evidence to determine the precise partial credits.

Second, to substantiate partner wage QREs under I.R.C. §§ 41(b)(2)(D) and 174(e), Vanguard's three equity partners must replace macro project time estimates with contemporaneous daily timeheets recording exact hours spent conducting or directly supervising technical experimentation on Sub-Components 2026-A, 2026-B, and 2026-C. At year-end, the partnership's tax advisor must prepare a contemporaneous Section 174(e) Independent Investor Valuation Memorandum computing partnership net income, partner capital accounts, and the annual return on equity under Exacto Spring Corp. v. Commissioner, 196 F.3d 833 (7th Cir. 1999), thereby locking in the rebuttable presumption of reasonableness that prevailed in Smith.
Case Study 2: Industrial Automation & Custom MEP Systems Firm — Net-Zero Thermal Recovery System Subject to Mid-Project Commercial Dispute Settlement
Baseline Project Scenario and Identified Smith Pitfalls

Apex Thermal & MEP Systems, Inc. ("Apex"), a domestic C-corporation specializing in custom mechanical, electrical, and industrial process engineering, enters into a $9.5 million engineering and prototype development agreement with a domestic hyperscale semiconductor manufacturer ("ChipCorp") to design an experimental two-phase liquid-immersion dielectric cooling and waste-heat recovery system. Midway through the Detailed Engineering phase, shifting thermal dissipation requirements and supply-chain bottlenecks trigger a major commercial dispute over unpaid invoices and scope modifications, leading Apex and ChipCorp to execute a mid-project Settlement and Contract Amendment Deed.

Under Apex's existing legal and accounting practices, the project suffers from three critical defects highlighted in the Smith opinion. First, the original contract compensated Apex on an hourly time-and-materials rate card subject to a ceiling, plus 100 percent reimbursement for laboratory fluid-dynamics test rigs. Under Smith (which, relying on Geosyntec and Dynetics, held that invoice-based percentage-of-completion payments, additional-service fees, and reimbursable expenses do not show financial risk contingent on research success) and Geosyntec (which held that a cost ceiling does not create the relevant risk), time-basis and reimbursable-expense billing places the financial risk of failed research on the client, failing Prong 1 of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1). Second, in the mid-project Settlement Deed, Apex agrees to accept a compromised lump-sum payout of $6.2 million to resolve $7.8 million in accumulated engineering costs and complete the prototype design. However, Apex's general counsel includes standard commercial release boilerplate stating: "For the avoidance of doubt, the Original Master Services Agreement remains in full force and effect subject to the Settlement Sum set forth herein." Under Judge Weiler's application of Large v. Mobile Tool International, Inc., 724 F.3d 766 (7th Cir. 2013), and Curia v. Nelson, 587 F.3d 824 (7th Cir. 2009), this preservation clause leaves the original non-contingent, time-based payment framework legally intact, and the $1.6 million commercial write-off is treated as an unrecoverable commercial compromise or loss of profit opportunity rather than financial risk contingent on research success. Third, although Apex spent $7.8 million in total project costs while receiving only $6.2 million under the Settlement Deed, its enterprise resource planning (ERP) system commingles routine CAD drafting, vendor procurement, and administrative project management in the same cost center as its thermodynamic R&D experimentation, rendering Apex unable to prove the exact amount of qualified research expenses that exceeded client payments under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3).
Step 1: Restructuring the Mid-Project Settlement Agreement Under Seventh Circuit Contract Modification Doctrine

To overcome the Tax Court's holdings under Large v. Mobile Tool International and Curia v. Nelson in Smith, Apex cannot execute a conventional commercial settlement release that preserves the underlying time-and-materials contract terms. Instead, when renegotiating a troubled engineering contract or drafting a Settlement Deed, legal counsel must structure the instrument as an express contractual novation that revokes the original time-based billing terms and replaces them with a fixed-price, technically contingent deliverable obligation.

First, Apex must delete the preservation boilerplate ("original contract remains in full force and effect") that appeared in the Masdar HQ Settlement Agreement and helped defeat the petitioners' settlement argument there (the Atrium City Tower Deed of Settlement, though it cancelled the remaining scope, likewise failed because it merely fixed payment for work completed). Second, Apex must condition its entitlement to earn and retain the $6.2 million settlement sum upon the cooling system prototype passing objective thermodynamic validation testing, while expressly confirming Apex's retention of substantial IP rights. Specifically, the Settlement Deed must incorporate the following superseding clauses:

"Section 3.1 (Express Novation of Payment Terms & Technical Contingency): Pursuant to the principles of contractual novation, the Parties hereby expressly revoke, supersede, and declare void ab initio all time-and-materials rate cards, hourly billing schedules, termination-for-time-spent clauses, and reimbursable expense provisions contained in Sections 4 and 12 of the Original Agreement. The Parties agree that the Revised Contract Sum of $6,200,000 constitutes a fixed-price, at-risk research and development commitment. Client's obligation to pay—and Apex's right to retain—the Revised Contract Sum is strictly contingent upon the Two-Phase Dielectric Cooling Prototype successfully achieving a validated Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) of [image4] and a continuous heat-flux dissipation rate of [image5] without dielectric fluid vapor-lock instability during the 72-Hour Acceptance Test Protocol set forth in Exhibit A. Any costs, wages, supplies, or testing expenditures incurred by Apex in excess of the Revised Contract Sum, or in re-engineering failed test iterations, shall be borne exclusively by Apex without recourse or reimbursement from Client."

"Section 3.2 (Confirmation of Substantial Rights in Research Results): Notwithstanding any prior agreement, all patents, trade secrets, thermodynamic equations, manifold geometries, pressure-regulation firmware, and empirical testing datasets generated by Apex ('Research Results') shall vest solely and exclusively in Apex. Client is granted a non-exclusive, royalty-free license to operate the installed prototype manifold strictly within Client's designated facility, and Apex retains the unrestricted, royalty-free right to manufacture, license, and commercially exploit the Research Results for any third party without Client's consent."
Step 2: Restructuring Contract Remedies to Align with State Commercial Law

In System Technologies, Inc. v. Commissioner, Docket No. 12211-21—a separate case on which the Smith petitioners relied—the Tax Court denied the Commissioner's motion for partial summary judgment because, where the contracts failed to provide an adequate remedy, Indiana's Uniform Commercial Code [UCC] (including its failure-of-essential-purpose rule) supplied the statutory remedy of a refund of amounts paid; in Smith, however, the Court distinguished that order, holding that foreign law does not override contracts that themselves provide adequate remedies and that, per Dynetics, risk is determined solely from the research agreement, without regard to any external statute not expressly incorporated in it. To reinforce Prong 1 compliance under domestic state law, Apex must expressly incorporate UCC Article 2 rejection, revocation of acceptance, and restitution remedies into its custom engineering contracts. Specifically, the contract must stipulate that if the custom thermal recovery system fails to meet the Exhibit A performance specifications during acceptance testing, any limitation-of-remedies clause is waived and ChipCorp is legally entitled to reject the tender and demand full restitution of all prior milestone payments, with zero carve-out for quantum meruit or work "properly performed" prior to rejection.
Step 3: Restructuring Project Governance and Financial Accounting for Partial Credit Substantiation (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3))

For any historical tax period prior to the execution of the Settlement Novation—where the IRS could argue that the original time-and-materials terms failed Prong 1 (payment contingency) while satisfying Prong 2 (substantial rights)—Apex must structure its project accounting so that it can prove the exact dollar amount of its partial research credit under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3) at trial without leaving the computation unresolved, as occurred in Smith.

To accomplish this, Apex's controller and R&D tax director must establish a Bifurcated Job-Cost Ledger within the ERP system that segregates every project expenditure into two mutually exclusive sub-accounts in real time. Sub-Account 101-Q (Qualified Research & Experimentation Costs) must capture solely W-2 engineering wages engaged in modeling, simulation, and prototype testing, physical prototype fabrication supplies, and 65 percent of domestic third-party laboratory testing fees directly incident to resolving thermodynamic uncertainty under I.R.C. § 41(d). Sub-Account 102-NQ (Non-Qualified Commercial & Production Costs) must isolate all routine CAD formatting, component procurement administration, commercial contract negotiations, site inspections, and post-validation production activities.

Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(ii) and (d)(2), when a taxpayer retains substantial rights under a funded contract, only the QREs that exceed total client payments received qualify for the credit. By maintaining a monthly reconciliation schedule mapping cumulative client payments ($6.2 million) directly against verified Sub-Account 101-Q expenditures ($7.1 million in pure QREs) and Sub-Account 102-NQ expenditures ($0.7 million in non-qualified costs), Apex can present the IRS exam team and the Tax Court with a self-contained, audit-ready schedule proving that its pure QREs ($7.1 million) exceeded total client funding ($6.2 million) by exactly $900,000. This accounting precision eliminates the evidentiary deficiency that prevented the Tax Court from computing the final partial credit award in Smith.
Step 4: Integrating Technical Documentation with Milestone Invoicing

Finally, to eliminate the evidentiary disconnect between engineering operations and commercial billing that undermined the taxpayers in Smith, Apex must synchronize its accounts-receivable invoicing with its technical experimentation tracking. In Smith, the Tax Court cited invoice-based, percentage-of-completion payment schedules—with no client review and approval of the work product required before payment, and clauses barring clients from delaying payment of the remainder of an invoice when an item was disputed—as evidence that the research was funded rather than contingent on research outcomes.

Apex must prohibit its billing department from issuing invoices that reference hourly labor increments (such as "Monthly Engineering Services — 620 Hours") or generic percentage-of-completion estimates ("75% Detailed Design Complete"). Instead, every commercial invoice issued under the contract must correspond to a numbered technical milestone in Exhibit A and must attach a formal Technical Benchmark Verification Certificate signed by both Apex's Chief Engineer and ChipCorp's Technical Representative certifying that the specific prototype subsystem achieved its quantitative thermodynamic performance metrics during laboratory testing. By compiling the executed contract novation, the sub-component simulation logs, the signed Technical Benchmark Verification Certificates, and the segregated Sub-Account 101-Q cost ledger into a unified contemporaneous trial binder, the taxpayer establishes an unassailable evidentiary record satisfying both I.R.C. § 41(d)(1) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d).

metaDescription: Smith v. Commissioner is a U.S. Tax Court ruling for architecture and engineering partnerships claiming the R&D tax credit under I.R.C. § 41.
